<section aria-labelledby="abstract"><h2 id="abstract">Abstract</h2>
<p class="paper-abstract">Grid interconnection has become a binding constraint on artificial intelligence (AI) data center development, yet existing planning frameworks do not price service that arrives later than planned. This paper develops the Cost of Delayed Energization (CoDE), a present-value framework that maps delayed information technology (IT) capacity to grid MW and MVA requirements and prices the delay separately for developers, ratepayers, and society. Two decision metrics, delay cost intensity and the break-even acceleration payment, make results comparable across project sizes, delays, and mitigation options. For a 300 MW-IT project delayed 36 months, private CoDE is 714 million USD, or 66.1 thousand USD per MW-IT-month, and committed-capital carrying cost keeps it above 1.0 billion USD at 60 months even as realization probability decays. A one-year natural-gas bridge over the same delay avoids 257 million USD of private cost while adding 25–68 million USD of expected climate damage, and the delay itself adds 25 million USD of ratepayer exposure. Because these third-party effects are smaller than the private values they are set against by factors of about four to thirty, the operative planning question is who should fund acceleration and how pathway externalities are compensated.</p>
<p class="paper-source">Abstract source: <a href="https://henryutd2021.github.io/files/papers/li2026code.pdf">PDF page 1</a>.</p></section>
